cards.title: 1.1 Historical Development of the Periodic Table (1/3)
body: **The Periodic Table of Elements is a systematic tabular arrangement of chemical elements organized by increasing atomic number, which highlights the recurring (periodic) chemical and physical properties of the elements.**

Classifying elements is crucial in chemistry. In the early 1800s, only about thirty elements were known, each with seemingly distinct properties. As new elements were discovered, scientists gathered more information, making it difficult to organize this knowledge. This led chemists to seek patterns, eventually giving rise to the modern Periodic Table, which provides a fundamental framework for understanding chemical behaviors.

Early classification attempts began by grouping elements simply into metals and nonmetals. In 1829, German chemist Johann Wolfgang Döbereiner attempted to organize elements into groups of three, known as **Döbereiner's Triads**. He noticed that when three elements with similar properties were written in order of increasing atomic mass, the atomic mass of the middle element was roughly the average of the other two. For example, in the triad of Lithium ($$6.9\text{ u}$$), Sodium ($$23.0\text{ u}$$), and Potassium ($$39.0\text{ u}$$), the average of Lithium and Potassium is $$\frac{6.9 + 39.0}{2} \approx 23.0\text{ u}$$, which matches Sodium. However, this triad system could not be applied to all elements and was of limited use.

In 1864, English chemist John Newlands arranged elements in order of increasing relative atomic mass and formulated the **Law of Octaves**. He observed that every eighth element exhibited similar physical and chemical properties, similar to the octaves found in music. While innovative, Newlands' system failed for elements beyond Calcium, as the pattern of eighth-element similarity did not hold for heavier elements.

cards.title: 1.1 Historical Development of the Periodic Table (2/3)
body: The major breakthrough in element classification belongs to Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev in 1869. Mendeleev organized the sixty-three known elements based on their atomic masses and chemical similarities, particularly their formulas when reacting with oxygen and hydrogen. He formulated **Mendeleev's Periodic Law**, which stated that the properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic masses. Mendeleev left empty gaps in his table for elements not yet discovered (such as *eka-Aluminium*), boldly predicting their physical and chemical properties. When Gallium was discovered later, its properties matched Mendeleev's predictions with remarkable accuracy.

Despite its success, Mendeleev's table had key limitations. It did not clearly place Hydrogen, could not accommodate isotopes (which have identical chemical properties but different masses), and contained mass-order discrepancies, such as placing Tellurium ($$127.6\text{ u}$$) before Iodine ($$126.9\text{ u}$$) to match their chemical families. These discrepancies were resolved in 1913 when English physicist Henry Moseley used X-ray spectra to prove that the **atomic number** (the number of protons in a nucleus) is the fundamental property of an element. This modified Mendeleev's law into the **Modern Periodic Law**: **The properties of elements are periodic functions of their atomic numbers.**

cards.title: Newlands — Law of Octaves
body: By the 1860s more elements were known, and chemists looked for repeating patterns. In 1864–1865 the English chemist John Newlands arranged known elements in order of increasing atomic mass.
Newlands noticed that every eighth element seemed to show properties similar to the first, like notes repeating every octave in music. He called this the Law of Octaves.
Example idea: if you list Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F, then Na (the 8th after Li in his listing) resembles lithium; K resembles sodium, and so on for the lighter elements.

Limitations: the law worked reasonably only for the lighter elements. It broke down for heavier elements; Newlands sometimes forced dissimilar elements into the same group to keep the octave pattern. New elements being discovered did not fit neatly. Many chemists rejected the musical analogy at first.
Despite its limits, Newlands helped establish that properties of elements repeat periodically when elements are ordered by mass — an important step toward the modern periodic table.

cards.title: Mendeleev’s periodic table
body: In 1869 the Russian chemist Dmitri Mendeleev arranged elements mainly in order of increasing atomic mass, but he also grouped elements with similar chemical properties into vertical columns (groups).

When the mass order conflicted with chemical similarity, Mendeleev sometimes adjusted positions. Crucially, he left gaps for elements that had not yet been discovered, and he predicted their properties (for example eka-silicon, later germanium; eka-aluminium, later gallium).
When gallium and germanium were discovered, their properties closely matched Mendeleev’s predictions. That success convinced many scientists that the periodic law was real.

Limitations of Mendeleev’s table: a few pairs of elements appeared in the wrong order if sorted strictly by atomic mass (e.g. tellurium and iodine; argon and potassium) because the true ordering principle had not yet been found. He also did not know about noble gases at first, and isotopes were unknown.

Contrast with Moseley: in 1913 Henry Moseley used X-ray spectra to show that nuclear charge (atomic number $$Z$$) increases by one from element to element. The modern periodic law orders elements by atomic number, which fixes the misplaced pairs and matches electron structure.

Summary: Newlands saw a repeating “every 8th” pattern; Mendeleev built a practical table with gaps and predictions based on atomic mass and properties; Moseley replaced mass with atomic number as the fundamental order.

cards.title: Historical development — from triads to atomic number
body: Döbereiner’s triads (1829): groups of three similar elements where the middle atomic mass was roughly the average of the other two (e.g. Li, Na, K; Cl, Br, I). This was an early hint of regularity, but only a few triads worked.
Newlands’ octaves: ordered by atomic mass; similarity every eighth element; failed for heavier elements.
Mendeleev: ordered by atomic mass with chemical groups, left gaps, predicted undiscovered elements; most successful 19th-century table.
Modern table (after Moseley): ordered by atomic number; periods and groups reflect electron configuration. Atomic mass still appears on the table, but atomic number decides position.

cards.title: 1.4.5 Valency and the pattern of formulas, step by step
body: **Valency** is the **bonding capacity** of an atom: the number of electrons it loses, gains or shares when it bonds. Because the group number tells you the valence electrons, it also tells you the valency.

**Step 1 — Read the valency from the group.** Groups I, II, III → valency **1, 2, 3** (they tend to **lose** electrons). Group IV → **4** (tends to **share**). Groups V, VI, VII → **3, 2, 1** (they tend to **gain or share**: 8 − group number).
**Step 2 — Write the symbols with their valencies.** e.g. aluminium (Al, 3) and chlorine (Cl, 1).
**Step 3 — Swap (criss-cross) the valencies** to become the subscripts of the other element: Al₁Cl₃.
**Step 4 — Simplify and drop the 1s:** AlCl₃. If both numbers can be divided by the same number, divide: Mg (2) + O (2) → Mg₂O₂ → **MgO**.
**Step 5 — Check:** total valency of each side must be equal: Al 1 × 3 = 3, Cl 3 × 1 = 3 ✔.

**The pattern:** across a period the formulas of the chlorides follow the valency: NaCl, MgCl₂, AlCl₃, SiCl₄, PCl₃, SCl₂, Cl₂. Elements in the **same group** have the **same pattern**: LiCl, NaCl, KCl; CCl₄, SiCl₄, GeCl₄. So if you know one formula in a group you can predict the others.

cards.title: 1.3 Electron Configuration and the Periodic Table (1/3)
body: **Electron configuration is the detailed distribution of an atom's electrons among various atomic orbitals and subshells in accordance with established energetic principles like the Aufbau principle.**

To understand why elements show periodic patterns, we must examine their electron configurations. In grade nine, we learned that electrons reside in main energy levels or shells ($$n = 1, 2, 3...$$ or K, L, M, N). In grade ten, we dive deeper: each main energy shell consists of one or more **subshells** designated by the letters **$$s, p, d, f$$**. The number of subshells in a shell is equal to its principal quantum number ($$n$$). For example, the first shell ($$n=1$$) has only one subshell ($$1s$$), while the second shell ($$n=2$$) has two subshells ($$2s$$ and $$2p$$).

Each subshell has a maximum capacity of electrons: an $$s$$ subshell can hold up to 2 electrons, a $$p$$ subshell can hold up to 6, a $$d$$ subshell up to 10, and an $$f$$ subshell up to 14. The total electron capacity of a main shell is determined by the formula **$$2n^2$$**.

cards.title: 1.3 Electron Configuration and the Periodic Table (2/3)
body: Electrons fill subshells in order of increasing energy. This filling order, known as the **Aufbau Principle**, is illustrated by a diagonal rule: $$1s \rightarrow 2s \rightarrow 2p \rightarrow 3s \rightarrow 3p \rightarrow 4s \rightarrow 3d \rightarrow 4p \rightarrow 5s...$$ Note that the $$4s$$ subshell is filled before the $$3d$$ subshell because $$4s$$ represents a slightly lower energy state than $$3d$$. For example, the configuration of Iron ($$Z = 26$$) is written as: $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^6 4s^2 3d^6$$.

To simplify writing configurations for heavier elements, we can use the **abbreviated electron configuration** (noble gas notation). This uses the symbol of the preceding noble gas in brackets to represent the core electrons. For instance, Sodium ($$Z = 11$$), which has the full configuration $$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^1$$, can be abbreviated as **$$[\text{Ne}]3s^1$$**, where $$[\text{Ne}]$$ represents the core configuration of Neon ($$1s^2 2s^2 2p^6$$).

Based on their outermost subshell configurations, elements are classified into three major blocks on the Periodic Table: • **Representative Elements (s-block and p-block):** These elements belong to Groups IA through VIIIA. Their outermost electrons are filling $$s$$ or $$p$$ subshells. For example, Lithium ($$1s^2 2s^1$$) is an s-block representative element, while Carbon ($$1s^2 2s^2 2p^2$$) is a p-block representative element. • **Transition Elements (d-block):** Located in the center of the Periodic Table (Groups IB through VIIIB). Their outermost occupied configurations are filling the $$d$$ subshell of the $$(n-1)$$ shell.

For example, Iron ($$[\text{Ar}]4s^2 3d^6$$) is a d-block transition element. • **Inner Transition Elements (f-block):** Shown in two rows below the main body of the table. Their electrons fill the $$f$$ subshell of the $$(n-2)$$ shell. These consist of the **Lanthanide** (filling $$4f$$) and **Actinide** (filling $$5f$$) series.

cards.title: 1.3 Electron Configuration and the Periodic Table (3/3)
body: > **💡 Did You Know?**: The subshell letters $$s, p, d, f$$ do not stand for shapes. They were originally named by early spectroscopists to describe spectral lines: **s**harp, **p**rincipal, **d**iffuse, and **f**undamental!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: To easily write noble gas configurations, find the noble gas in the row directly *above* the element you are working on, place its symbol in brackets, and then continue filling subshells for the element's own row.

cards.title: 1.4 Periodic Regularities and Characteristics of Elements
body: **Periodic trends are the predictable, systematic variations in the physical and chemical properties of elements across periods and down groups of the Periodic Table.**

The arrangement of elements by atomic number reveals clear, repeating patterns in their physical and chemical behaviors. These regularities are governed by the balance between the nuclear charge attracting the electrons and the shielding effect of the core electrons.

cards.title: 1.4 Periodic Regularities and Characteristics of Elements — Core Periodic Trends (1/2)
body: • **Atomic Radius:** The distance from the center of the nucleus to the outermost occupied electron shell. • *Down a Group:* Atomic radius **increases**. Although nuclear charge increases, new energy shells are added, which increases the physical distance and shielding of outer electrons, overcoming the nuclear pull. • *Across a Period:* Atomic radius **decreases**. The number of shells remains constant, but the atomic number (nuclear charge) increases.

This increased positive charge pulls the outer electrons closer, reducing the size. • **Ionic Radius:** Cations (positive ions) are always **smaller** than their parent atoms because losing valence electrons reduces electron-electron repulsion, allowing the nucleus to pull remaining electrons tighter. Anions (negative ions) are always **larger** than their parent atoms because gaining electrons increases electron-electron repulsion, expanding the electron cloud. • **Ionization Energy (IE):** The minimum energy required to remove the outermost electron from a neutral gaseous atom. • *Down a Group:* IE **decreases**.

Outer electrons are farther from the nucleus and heavily shielded by core electrons, making them easier to remove. • *Across a Period:* IE **increases**. As atomic size decreases and nuclear charge increases, the nucleus holds outer electrons more tightly, requiring more energy to remove them. • **Electronegativity (EN):** A measure of an atom's ability to attract shared electrons in a chemical bond. • *Down a Group:* EN **decreases**. The shared electrons are farther from the attractive pull of the positive nucleus. • *Across a Period:* EN **increases** (excluding noble gases).

The smaller atomic size and higher nuclear charge allow the nucleus to exert a stronger pull on shared electrons. • **Metallic and Nonmetallic Characteristics:** Metals tend to lose electrons (low IE, low EN), while nonmetals tend to gain electrons (high IE, high EN). Metallic character **increases down a group** and **decreases across a period**, while nonmetallic character follows the opposite trend.

cards.title: 1.4 Periodic Regularities and Characteristics of Elements — Core Periodic Trends (2/2)
body: These properties also affect the chemical formulas of compounds formed across periods. For example, chlorides of period 3 elements show a distinct pattern based on valency. Group IA Sodium forms $$NaCl$$, Group IIA Magnesium forms $$MgCl_2$$, and Group IIIA Aluminium forms $$AlCl_3$$. As we transition to covalent nonmetals, Group IVA Silicon forms $$SiCl_4$$, and Group VA Phosphorus forms $$PCl_3$$. This periodic change in formulas directly reflects the valence electron configurations of the elements.

> **💡 Did You Know?**: Fluorine ($$F$$) is the most electronegative element on the Pauling scale with a value of $$4.0$$, while Francium ($$Fr$$) and Cesium ($$Cs$$) are the least electronegative at $$0.7$$!

> **🧠 Pro-Tip**: Remember the acronym **AIE**: **A**tomic radius trends are opposite to those of **I**onization energy and **E**lectronegativity. If atomic size increases, both IE and EN will decrease.

tips.text: Many scientists made several attempts to classify the elements according to their properties and obtain an orderly arrangement of elements.

The elements in the same group were called families. Each horizontal row in the periodic table is called a period. There are seven periods and the period number usually represents number of electron shells that which a given element possesses.
The vertical column in the periodic table is called a group.
Elements in a group have similar chemical properties because they contain the same number of valence electrons.
The electron shells consist of one or more subshells that are denoted by the letters s, p, d, and f.
Transitions elements are found in the center of the periodic table and are denoted by a letter B.
The two long rows which are located below the main body of the table are called inner transition elements.
The modern periodic table is widely used to predict the physical and the chemical properties and the periodic regularities of the elements.
The atomic radius of an atom is the distance from the centre of the nucleus to the outermost shell.
The atomic radius can be calculated by measuring the distances between the nuclei of atoms in the chemical bonds of molecular substances.

units.title: Chemical Bonding and Forces of Attraction
units.intro: Atoms stick because electrons are shared or transferred.

cards.title: 2.1 Forces of Attractions
body: **Chemical bonds** are the forces of attraction that hold atoms together: can be described as attractive forces.
Intramolecular bonds refer to the forces of attraction that hold atoms together within a molecule.
Generally, intramolecular forces are considerably stronger than intermolecular forces.

cards.title: Step by step: Forces of attraction
body: **Step 1:** Intramolecular forces (chemical bonds) hold atoms together inside a substance: ionic (transfer of electrons, metal + non-metal), covalent (sharing of electron pairs, non-metals) and metallic (cations in a sea of delocalized electrons).
**Step 2:** Intermolecular forces act between separate molecules and are much weaker than bonds.
**Step 3:** London (dispersion) forces exist between all molecules and grow with molecular size.
**Step 4:** Dipole–dipole forces act between polar molecules (e.g. HCl); hydrogen bonds are especially strong dipole forces when H is bonded to N, O or F (e.g. H₂O, NH₃, HF).
**Step 5:** Stronger intermolecular forces → higher melting and boiling points.
**Example:** Water (M = 18) boils at 100 °C while hydrogen sulphide H₂S (M = 34) boils at −60 °C: water molecules are held by hydrogen bonds, H₂S molecules only by weaker dipole and London forces.

cards.title: 2.2.3 Polar and Non polar Covalent Bonds
body: A **Polar covalent bond** is a covalent bond in which the electrons are not equally shared.
The more electronegative atom attracts the shared electron pairs more than the one with less electronegative value.
The Cl atom has the higher electronegativity so the electrons are drawn more towards the Cl atom and away from the H atom.
Since electrons carry a negative charge, this gives the Cl atom a partial negative charge.

cards.title: From polar bonds to polar molecules, step by step
body: A **polar bond** has a partly negative end (δ−) and a partly positive end (δ+) because the two atoms have different **electronegativities**. A **polar molecule** has a δ− side and a δ+ side **overall**. A molecule can contain polar bonds and still be non-polar — the **shape** decides.

**Step 1 — Compare electronegativities (EN) for each bond.** ΔEN ≈ 0 → non-polar covalent bond (H–H, Cl–Cl, C–H is nearly non-polar). Small to moderate ΔEN → polar covalent bond (H–Cl, O–H, C=O). Large ΔEN (about 1.7–2 or more) → ionic bond (Na⁺Cl⁻). The change is gradual (textbook Fig 2.2).
**Step 2 — Draw each bond dipole** as an arrow from δ+ towards δ− (towards the more electronegative atom).
**Step 3 — Work out the shape.** Count the bonding pairs and lone pairs on the central atom: CO₂ linear, H₂O bent, NH₃ pyramidal, CH₄ and CCl₄ tetrahedral, BF₃ trigonal planar.
**Step 4 — Add the arrows.** If the shape is **symmetrical** and all outer atoms are the same, the bond dipoles cancel → **non-polar molecule**. If not, they leave a net dipole → **polar molecule**.
The textbook explains bond polarity (2.2.3); deciding the polarity of a whole molecule from its shape is added here because exam questions ask it.
**Shortcut:** a **lone pair on the central atom** (H₂O, NH₃, SO₂) almost always makes the molecule polar; symmetrical molecules with identical outer atoms (CO₂, CH₄, CCl₄, BF₃) are non-polar.

cards.title: Model: polar and non-polar molecules

steps.text: **HCl** — one polar bond, nothing to cancel it → **polar** molecule. Cl is δ−, H is δ+.
**H₂O** — two polar O–H bonds in a **bent** shape (104.5°). The arrows both point up towards O and add → **polar**.
**CO₂** — two polar C=O bonds, but the molecule is **linear**: equal arrows point in opposite directions and cancel → **non-polar**.
**CH₄** — four C–H bonds in a symmetrical **tetrahedron**; the small dipoles cancel → **non-polar**.

body: Tap each molecule: the arrows show the bond dipoles.

cards.title: How polarity shows up in real life
body: **Charged rod test:** hold a rubbed plastic ruler near a thin stream of water — the stream **bends** towards it (polar). A stream of hexane or CCl₄ does not bend (non-polar).
**“Like dissolves like”:** polar and ionic substances dissolve in polar water (salt, sugar, ethanol); non-polar substances dissolve in non-polar solvents (grease and oil in kerosene).
**Boiling points:** for molecules of similar size, polar molecules have **higher** boiling points because dipole–dipole attractions add to London forces.

cards.title: Worked example: is NH₃ polar? is CCl₄ polar?
cards.problem: Decide whether ammonia, NH₃, and carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄, are polar molecules.

steps.text: NH₃: N (EN 3.0) is more electronegative than H (2.1) → three polar N–H bonds, N is δ−.
N has 3 bonding pairs + 1 lone pair → trigonal **pyramidal**, not symmetrical.
The three dipoles all point up towards N and do not cancel → NH₃ is **polar**.
CCl₄: Cl (3.0) is more electronegative than C (2.5) → four polar C–Cl bonds.
C has 4 bonding pairs, no lone pair → regular **tetrahedron** with four identical outer atoms.
The four dipoles cancel exactly → CCl₄ is **non-polar** (even though every bond is polar).

cards.answer: NH₃ polar (pyramidal, lone pair); CCl₄ non-polar (symmetrical tetrahedron).

cards.title: Worked example: CO₂ vs SO₂
cards.problem: CO₂ is non-polar but SO₂ is polar, although both have two polar bonds to oxygen. Explain.

steps.text: Both have polar bonds: O is more electronegative than C and than S.
CO₂: C has no lone pair → **linear** O=C=O; the two dipoles are equal and opposite → cancel.
SO₂: S has a lone pair → **bent** shape; the two dipoles point partly the same way → net dipole.

cards.answer: Shape decides: linear CO₂ cancels, bent SO₂ does not.

cards.title: 2.2.5 Metallic bonding, step by step
body: **Metallic bonding** is the attraction between **positive metal ions** and the **delocalised (free-moving) valence electrons** around them. It holds metals together in the solid.
**Step 1 — Metal atoms lose their valence electrons easily** (low ionisation energy). Sodium gives 1 electron per atom, magnesium 2, aluminium 3.
**Step 2 — The atoms become positive ions (cations)** packed in regular layers (a lattice).
**Step 3 — The released electrons are delocalised:** they do not belong to one atom or one bond; they move freely through the whole metal, like a “sea” of electrons.
**Step 4 — The bond:** every cation is attracted to the electron sea and the sea is attracted to every cation. This attraction acts in **all directions**, so the bond is **non-directional**.

**What makes it stronger?** More delocalised electrons per atom, a higher ion charge and a smaller ion → stronger attraction → higher melting point. Example: Na (1 e⁻) melts at 98 °C, Mg (2 e⁻) at 650 °C, Al (3 e⁻) at 660 °C.

**Note on the textbook model (Fig. 2.3):** the circles labelled “positive nucleus” are really **positive metal ions** — each is a nucleus **plus its inner electrons**; only the valence electrons are in the sea.

cards.problem: Explain why the melting point rises from sodium (98 °C) to magnesium (650 °C) and aluminium (660 °C).

steps.text: Na gives **1**, Mg **2** and Al **3** delocalised electrons per atom.
The ions also become more highly charged (Na⁺, Mg²⁺, Al³⁺) and smaller.
More electrons in the sea + higher charge + smaller ions → stronger attraction between ions and electrons.
More energy is needed to loosen the lattice → higher melting point.

cards.answer: The metallic bond gets stronger from Na to Al.

cards.title: Worked example: why a metal conducts but solid salt does not
cards.problem: Copper conducts electricity as a solid; sodium chloride conducts only when molten or dissolved. Explain.

steps.text: A current needs **charged particles that can move**.
In copper the delocalised electrons are free to move even in the solid → conducts.
In solid NaCl the ions are locked in the lattice and there are no free electrons → no current.
When NaCl melts or dissolves, the ions become free to move → conducts.

cards.answer: Metals have mobile electrons; ionic solids have fixed ions.

cards.title: Worked example: hammering a metal and a salt
cards.problem: Why does a piece of copper flatten when hammered, while a crystal of salt shatters?

steps.text: In copper, the layers of Cu²⁺ ions slide over each other; the electron sea still surrounds every ion, so the bond is not broken → it flattens.
In NaCl, a slight shift brings ions of the **same charge** next to each other (+ next to +, − next to −).
The like charges repel and the crystal splits → brittle.

cards.answer: Metallic bonding is non-directional; ionic lattices break when like charges meet.

cards.title: London (dispersion) forces, step by step
body: London forces (dispersion forces) are the **weakest** intermolecular forces, but they act between **all** molecules and atoms — and they are the **only** attraction between non-polar molecules and noble-gas atoms.
**Step 1 — Electrons move.** In a non-polar molecule the electron cloud is evenly spread *on average*, but at any instant it may be a little more on one side.
**Step 2 — Instantaneous dipole.** For that instant the molecule has a δ− side and a δ+ side.
**Step 3 — Induced dipole.** That tiny dipole pushes or pulls the electrons of the neighbouring molecule, creating a dipole in it, lined up so that δ+ faces δ−.
**Step 4 — Attraction.** The two short-lived dipoles attract. Millions of these flickering attractions together hold the molecules (Fig 2.10: two iodine molecules).

**What makes them stronger?** (1) **More electrons / bigger molecules** — a large electron cloud is easily distorted (more polarisable). (2) **Larger contact area** — long, straight molecules touch more than compact, round ones.

cards.title: How to classify an unknown solid
body: Ask four school tests: melting point high or low? Does the solid conduct? Does the melt/solution conduct? Does it dissolve in water? High melt + conducts only when molten/dissolved → ionic. High melt + never conducts + insoluble → giant covalent. Low melt + never conducts → simple molecular. Conducts as a solid and bends → metal.

Dot-and-cross: metals lose until they look noble; non-metals gain or share until they look noble. MgCl₂ needs two Cl because Mg gives two electrons. Covalent pairs sit between symbols; leftover dots are lone pairs. Lone pairs push — that is why water is bent and ammonia is pyramidal (named properly in Grade 12).

Hydrogen bonding is a special strong intermolecular force, not a fourth primary bond. It explains water’s high boiling point, ice floating, and DNA later. units.intro: Solution = solute + solvent, homogeneous. Dilute vs concentrated is amount, not “how dangerous”. Saturated: no more solute dissolves at that T. Solubility usually rises with T for solids; gases dissolve better when cold and under pressure.

cards.title: Formula
body: concentration = amount of solute / volume of solution
School: mol/dm³ or g/dm³. Same units top and bottom.

cards.title: Making and talking about a solution
body: Always say the temperature when you quote solubility — “35 g per 100 g water at 20 °C” is a complete sentence; “35 g” is not. A solubility curve slopes up for most solids; a point above the curve is supersaturated, on the curve saturated, below unsaturated.

Concentration arithmetic: convert cm³ to dm³ (÷1000) before you divide. Diluting: moles of solute stay put, only volume grows, so c₁V₁ = c₂V₂. Stirring and powdering speed dissolving; they do not raise the saturated amount — only temperature (for most solids) does that.
Electrolytes: ionic or strong-acid solutions. Non-electrolytes: sugar, ethanol. Weak electrolytes: weak acids that only partly split. That vocabulary prepares Unit 4.

cards.title: 3.1.1 Describing Solutions
body: A solution is composed of a solute and a solvent.
**A solvent** is the substance that dissolves the solute.
The material dissolved is called a **solute**.
Solids, liquids and gases can dissolve in a solvent.

**Step 3: Final Answer**

**Step 1: Understand solid solutions**
Solid-in-solid solutions are called alloys, formed by mixing melted metals and allowing them to solidify.

**Step 2: Identify the alloy**

**Step 3: Final Answer**

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: How does temperature affect the solubility of most gaseous solutes in liquid solvents?
cards.why:
**Step 1: Analyze gas dissolution thermodynamics**
Dissolving gas in a liquid is an exothermic process. According to Le Chatelier's principle, adding heat shifts the equilibrium to favor the un-dissolved gas phase.

**Step 2: Connect to particle kinetic energy**
At higher temperatures, gas molecules have higher kinetic energy, allowing them to break weak intermolecular attractions with solvent molecules and escape as gas.

**Step 3: Final Answer**
Therefore, gas solubility **decreases as temperature increases**.

cards.title: Five ways to express concentration
body: Concentration tells you **how much solute** is in a given amount of **solution** (or solvent). Learn each formula with its units:
$$\text{mass \%} = \frac{\text{mass of solute}}{\text{mass of solution}} \times 100$$
$$\text{volume \%} = \frac{\text{volume of solute}}{\text{volume of solution}} \times 100$$
$$M = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{V_{\text{solution}}\,(\text{L})} \quad (\text{mol/L})$$
$$m = \frac{n_{\text{solute}}}{\text{mass of solvent (kg)}} \quad (\text{mol/kg})$$
$$N = \frac{\text{number of equivalents}}{V_{\text{solution}}\,(\text{L})} = M \times (\text{replaceable H}^+ \text{ or OH}^-)$$
Always find the **moles** first: \(n = \dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{molar mass}}\).

cards.title: Concentration units at a glance
head: Unit
Symbol
Per …
SI-type units
Changes with temperature?
body: Molality and mass percent use only masses, so they do not change when the solution warms up — that is why molality is used for boiling-point elevation.

steps.text: Everything goes through **moles of solute**: n = mass ÷ molar mass.
**Molarity**: divide moles by litres of **solution**.
**Molality**: divide moles by kilograms of **solvent** (not solution).
**Normality**: multiply molarity by the number of replaceable H⁺ (acid) or OH⁻ (base).
**Mass percent**: needs masses only. To switch between percent and molarity you also need the **density** of the solution.

cards.title: Mass percent, step by step
body: 1. Find the mass of solute and the mass of **solution** (solution = solute + solvent).
2. Divide and multiply by 100.
“A 10% salt solution” means 10 g of salt in every 100 g of solution, i.e. 10 g salt + 90 g water.

cards.title: Worked example: mass percent
cards.problem: 25 g of sodium chloride is dissolved in 100 g of water. Find the mass percent of NaCl.

steps.text: Mass of solution = 25 g + 100 g = 125 g (do not forget to add the solute).
\(\text{mass \%} = \dfrac{25}{125} \times 100\)

cards.title: Worked example: making a solution of given mass percent
cards.problem: How many grams of KNO₃ and of water are needed to make 250 g of an 8.0 % (by mass) KNO₃ solution?

steps.text: Mass of solute = \(\dfrac{8.0}{100} \times 250 \text{ g}\) = 20 g KNO₃
Mass of water = 250 g − 20 g = 230 g

cards.answer: 20 g KNO₃ dissolved in 230 g water

cards.title: Volume percent, step by step
body: Used when both solute and solvent are **liquids** (alcohol in water, antiseptics).
1. Find the volume of the liquid solute and the total volume of **solution**.
2. Divide and multiply by 100.
**Careful:** volumes are not always additive — 50 mL ethanol + 50 mL water gives a little **less** than 100 mL. Use the measured volume of solution.

cards.title: Worked example: volume percent
cards.problem: How much pure ethanol is in 500 mL of a 70 % (v/v) ethanol hand-sanitiser solution?

steps.text: Volume of ethanol = \(\dfrac{70}{100} \times 500 \text{ mL}\)
= 350 mL ethanol (the rest, about 150 mL, is water)

cards.title: Molarity, step by step
body: 1. Convert the mass of solute into **moles**: n = m ÷ M.
2. Convert the volume of **solution** into **litres** (mL ÷ 1000).
3. \(M = \dfrac{n}{V}\). Rearranged: \(n = M \times V\) and mass = \(M \times V \times\) molar mass.
**Dilution:** adding water does not change the moles of solute, so \(M_1V_1 = M_2V_2\) (textbook 3.2.2, p.92).

cards.title: Worked example: molarity from mass
cards.problem: 11.7 g of NaCl (M = 58.5 g/mol) is dissolved in water to make 500 mL of solution. Find the molarity.

steps.text: Volume: 500 mL = 0.500 L

cards.title: Worked example: mass needed for a molar solution
cards.problem: What mass of NaOH (M = 40 g/mol) is needed to make 250 mL of 0.20 M solution?

steps.text: Moles needed: \(n = M \times V = 0.20 \times 0.250 = 0.050\text{ mol}\)
Mass: \(0.050 \times 40 = 2.0\text{ g}\)
Dissolve 2.0 g NaOH in a little water, then add water up to the 250 mL mark of a volumetric flask.

cards.title: Worked example: dilution
cards.problem: What volume of 2.0 M HCl is needed to make 500 mL of 0.10 M HCl?

steps.text: \(2.0 \times V_1 = 0.10 \times 500\text{ mL}\)
Measure 25 mL of 2.0 M HCl and add water to make 500 mL (add acid to water, never water to acid).

cards.title: Molality, step by step
body: 1. Find the moles of solute.
2. Find the mass of **solvent** only, in **kilograms** (g ÷ 1000).
3. \(m = \dfrac{n_{\text{solute}}}{\text{kg of solvent}}\)
**Molarity vs molality:** molarity divides by litres of **solution**; molality divides by kilograms of **solvent**. For dilute water solutions the two numbers are almost equal (1 L of water ≈ 1 kg).

cards.title: Worked example: molality
cards.problem: 10.0 g of NaOH (M = 40 g/mol) is dissolved in 500 g of water. Find the molality.

steps.text: Moles: \(n = \dfrac{10.0}{40} = 0.250\text{ mol}\)
Solvent: 500 g = 0.500 kg

cards.title: Worked example: molality of urea
cards.problem: 6.0 g of urea, CO(NH₂)₂ (M = 60 g/mol), is dissolved in 200 g of water. Find the molality.

cards.title: Normality, step by step
body: Normality counts **equivalents** — for acids and bases, the moles of H⁺ or OH⁻ that can react.

1. **Equivalent mass** of an acid = \(\dfrac{\text{molar mass}}{\text{number of replaceable H}}\); of a base = \(\dfrac{\text{molar mass}}{\text{number of OH}}\). HCl: 36.5 g; H₂SO₄: 98 ÷ 2 = 49 g; NaOH: 40 g; Ca(OH)₂: 74 ÷ 2 = 37 g.
2. Equivalents = \(\dfrac{\text{mass}}{\text{equivalent mass}}\).
3. \(N = \dfrac{\text{equivalents}}{V(\text{L})}\) — or simply \(N = M \times\) (number of replaceable H⁺ or OH⁻) (textbook p.91).
So 1 M HCl = 1 N, but 1 M H₂SO₄ = 2 N and 1 M H₃PO₄ = 3 N (if all three H react).

cards.title: Worked example: normality of sulfuric acid
cards.problem: 4.9 g of H₂SO₄ (M = 98 g/mol) is dissolved to make 500 mL of solution. Find (a) the molarity and (b) the normality.

steps.text: Moles: \(n = \dfrac{4.9}{98} = 0.050\text{ mol}\)
H₂SO₄ has 2 replaceable H → equivalent mass = 49 g; equivalents = 4.9 ÷ 49 = 0.10

cards.title: Worked example: normality of bases
cards.problem: Find the normality of (a) 0.50 M NaOH and (b) 0.10 M Ca(OH)₂.

steps.text: (a) NaOH gives 1 OH⁻ → N = 0.50 × 1 = 0.50 N
(b) Ca(OH)₂ gives 2 OH⁻ → N = 0.10 × 2 = 0.20 N

cards.title: Converting between units, step by step
body: **Mass % ⇄ molarity** needs the **density** of the solution. Work with a convenient amount: **1 L of solution** (its mass = density × 1000 mL).
**Molarity → molality:** take 1 L of solution, find its mass (density), subtract the mass of solute → mass of solvent, then divide moles by kg of solvent.
**Mass % → molality:** take 100 g of solution: solute grams = the percent, solvent = 100 − percent.
**Molarity ⇄ normality:** N = M × (H⁺ or OH⁻ per formula).

cards.title: Worked example: concentrated HCl
cards.problem: Concentrated hydrochloric acid is 36.5 % HCl by mass and has density 1.18 g/mL. Find its molarity and molality (HCl = 36.5 g/mol).

steps.text: Take 1 L = 1000 mL of solution: mass = 1000 × 1.18 = 1180 g.
Mass of HCl = 36.5 % of 1180 g = 430.7 g.
Moles of HCl = \(\dfrac{430.7}{36.5} = 11.8\text{ mol}\) → molarity = **11.8 M**.
Molality = \(\dfrac{11.8}{0.7493} = 15.7\text{ mol/kg}\).

cards.title: Worked example: from molarity to molality and mass %
cards.problem: A 2.00 M NaCl solution has density 1.08 g/mL. Find its molality and mass percent (NaCl = 58.5 g/mol).

steps.text: 1 L of solution has mass 1080 g and contains 2.00 mol NaCl.
Mass of NaCl = 2.00 × 58.5 = 117 g.
Mass of water = 1080 − 117 = 963 g = 0.963 kg.

cards.title: Memory trick: big M, small m
body: **Big M** = the big flask (whole **solution**, litres). **Small m** = the small bit that is only **solvent** (kilograms). **N** = **N**umber of H⁺/OH⁻ times M.

cards.title: Tips and common mistakes
body: Change **mL → L** for M and N, and **g → kg** for molality.
Mass % uses mass of **solution** (solute + solvent) on the bottom; molality uses mass of **solvent** only.
Write the units at every step — the units tell you which formula you are using.
For any conversion between % and M you need the **density**.

cards.title: Step by step: Calculations involving solutions
body: **Step 1:** Molarity (M) = moles of solute ÷ volume of solution in litres (mol/L).
**Step 2:** Moles = mass ÷ molar mass, so mass needed = M × V(L) × molar mass.
**Step 3:** Mass percent = (mass of solute ÷ mass of solution) × 100 %; mass of solution = solute + solvent.
**Step 4:** Dilution: the moles of solute stay the same, so M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
**Step 5:** Always convert mL to L (÷ 1000) before using molarity.

**Example:** Mass of NaOH (M = 40 g/mol) to make 250 mL of 0.20 M solution: n = 0.20 mol/L × 0.250 L = 0.050 mol; mass = 0.050 × 40 = 2.0 g. Dilution: 50 mL of 2.0 M HCl diluted to 500 mL → M₂ = 2.0 × 50/500 = 0.20 M.

cards.title: 3.3.1 Dissolution of Solutes in Liquids
body: Because the intermolecular forces in both the solute and the solvent are similar, it is easy for the intermolecular forces in the solute to be broken, allowing the solute to move into the spaces between the molecules of the solvent.
The effect of the polarity of the molecules is also noticeable when gases dissolve in water.
H2 and O2 are nonpolar, whereas NH3 and HCl are polar.

cards.title: 3.3.2 Effect of Temperature and Pressure on Solubility
body: The effect of pressure on gas solubility is used in the preparation of carbonated beverages.

cards.title: 3.3.3 Colligative Properties of Solutions
body: The properties of solutions can be divided into two main groups: colligative and non-colligative properties.
Non-colligative are those that depend on the identity of the dissolved solute and the solvent.
All physical properties of a solution that depend on the number of solute particles dissolved in the solution are called **colligative properties**.
**Vaporization** is a process in which a liquid is converted to a vapour.

cards.title: Boiling point elevation, step by step
body: **Boiling** happens when the vapour pressure of a liquid equals the atmospheric pressure. Pure water at sea level boils at 100 °C.
**Step 1 — Solute lowers the vapour pressure.** Non-volatile solute particles take up part of the surface, so fewer solvent molecules escape per second.
**Step 2 — More heating is needed.** At 100 °C the solution’s vapour pressure is still below atmospheric pressure, so it does not boil yet.
**Step 3 — The solution boils higher.** It must be heated above 100 °C until its vapour pressure reaches atmospheric pressure. The rise is the **boiling point elevation**, ΔTb.
$$\Delta T_b = T_b(\text{solution}) - T_b(\text{solvent}) = K_b \times m$$

Kb is the **molal boiling point constant** of the solvent (water: 0.52 °C kg/mol) and m is the **molality**. ΔTb depends only on the **number** of solute particles, not on what they are — it is a **colligative property**.
**Ionic solutes (extension):** NaCl splits into Na⁺ and Cl⁻, so 1 mol gives about 2 mol of particles and roughly doubles ΔTb. CaCl₂ gives 3 particles.

cards.title: Model: why a solution boils higher

steps.text: **Pure water** boils at 100 °C: its vapour pressure reaches 1 atm (760 mmHg).
The **solution** (blue) has a lower vapour pressure at every temperature, so it reaches 1 atm only at a higher temperature.
The gap between the two boiling points is **ΔTb = Kb·m**.

cards.title: Worked example: boiling point of a sugar solution
cards.problem: Find the boiling point of a 0.40 m aqueous sugar solution (Kb of water = 0.52 °C kg/mol).

steps.text: \(\Delta T_b = K_b \times m = 0.52 \times 0.40\)
\(\Delta T_b = 0.208 \approx 0.21\,^\circ\text{C}\)
Boiling point = 100 + 0.21 = 100.21 °C

cards.title: Worked example: from grams to boiling point
cards.problem: 9.0 g of glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆ (M = 180 g/mol), is dissolved in 100 g of water. Find the boiling point of the solution.

steps.text: Moles of glucose: \(n = \dfrac{9.0}{180} = 0.050\text{ mol}\)
Molality: \(m = \dfrac{0.050}{0.100\text{ kg}} = 0.50\text{ mol/kg}\)
\(\Delta T_b = 0.52 \times 0.50 = 0.26\,^\circ\text{C}\)
Boiling point = 100.26 °C

cards.title: Worked example: molar mass from boiling point elevation
cards.problem: 3.0 g of a non-volatile, non-electrolyte solute is dissolved in 50 g of benzene (Kb = 2.53 °C kg/mol). The boiling point rises by 0.60 °C. Find the molar mass of the solute.

steps.text: Molality: \(m = \dfrac{\Delta T_b}{K_b} = \dfrac{0.60}{2.53} = 0.237\text{ mol/kg}\)
Moles of solute = \(0.237 \times 0.050\text{ kg} = 0.0119\text{ mol}\)
Molar mass = \(\dfrac{3.0\text{ g}}{0.0119\text{ mol}} \approx 253\text{ g/mol}\)

cards.title: Osmosis and osmotic pressure, step by step
body: **Osmosis** is the movement of **solvent** (water) molecules through a **semi-permeable membrane** from a **dilute** solution (or pure water) into a **more concentrated** solution. The membrane lets water through but not the solute particles.
**Step 1 — Unequal water concentration.** Pure water has more free water molecules per volume than the solution, so more water crosses into the solution each second than comes back.
**Step 2 — The level rises.** The solution side gains water and its level rises in the tube (textbook Fig 3.9).
**Step 3 — Balance.** The extra weight of the raised column pushes water back. When the two flows are equal, osmosis stops.

**Osmotic pressure (π)** is the pressure that must be applied to the concentrated solution to **stop** osmosis. It is proportional to the height of the column and, like other colligative properties, depends on the **number** of solute particles.
**Formula (extension, beyond the textbook):** \(\pi = MRT\), with M in mol/L, R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K) and T in kelvin.

**Uses and examples:** a drip (infusion) must have the **same** osmotic pressure as blood (0.9 % NaCl, “isotonic”); red blood cells swell and burst in pure water and shrink in very salty water; salting meat or fish draws water out of germs and preserves the food; plant roots take in water by osmosis; **reverse osmosis** (pushing harder than π) makes drinking water from sea water.

states.label: Start
states.text: Pure water on the left, sugar solution on the right, same level. The membrane lets only water through.

states.label: Osmosis
states.text: More water moves right (into the solution) than left — the solution level rises.

states.label: Osmotic pressure
states.text: Pushing on the solution side with a pressure π stops the net flow: that pressure is the osmotic pressure.

cards.title: Worked example: osmotic pressure of glucose (extension)
cards.problem: Calculate the osmotic pressure of a 0.10 M glucose solution at 27 °C.

steps.text: \(\pi = MRT = 0.10 \times 0.0821 \times 300\)
\(\pi = 2.46\text{ atm}\)

cards.title: Worked example: which has the higher osmotic pressure?
cards.problem: Which has the higher osmotic pressure at the same temperature: 0.10 M glucose or 0.10 M NaCl? Which has the higher boiling point?

steps.text: Glucose does not ionise: 0.10 mol of particles per litre.
NaCl → Na⁺ + Cl⁻: about 0.20 mol of particles per litre.
Colligative properties depend on the number of particles → NaCl solution has the higher osmotic pressure **and** the higher boiling point.

cards.answer: 0.10 M NaCl (about twice as many particles) for both.

cards.title: Quick check
cards.q: What is the relationship between the solubility of a gaseous solute in a liquid and the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid (Henry's Law)?

options.A: Solubility is inversely proportional to pressure.
options.B: Solubility is directly proportional to pressure.
options.C: Pressure has no effect on gas solubility.

cards.why:
**Step 1: State Henry's Law**
Henry's Law states that at a constant temperature, the solubility of a gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the partial pressure of that gas above the liquid.

**Step 2: Final Answer**
Therefore, **Solubility is directly proportional to pressure.**

body: The sour taste of lemon and vinegar is due to the presence of different types of acids.
The same holds true for the sour taste of common fruits and vegetables.

cards.title: Arrhenius theory, step by step
body: **Acid:** a substance that produces **hydrogen ions, H⁺**, in water. **Base:** a substance that produces **hydroxide ions, OH⁻**, in water.
HCl(aq) → H⁺(aq) + Cl⁻(aq); H₂SO₄(aq) → 2H⁺(aq) + SO₄²⁻(aq); NaOH(aq) → Na⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq).
**Neutralisation** is then simply H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l).

**Limitations:** (1) it works only in **water**; (2) it cannot explain why **ammonia, NH₃**, is a base — NH₃ contains no OH; (3) a bare H⁺ does not exist in water — it is attached to a water molecule as **H₃O⁺** (hydronium ion).

cards.title: Brønsted–Lowry theory, step by step
body: **Acid = proton (H⁺) donor. Base = proton (H⁺) acceptor.** An acid–base reaction is a **proton transfer**.
**Step 1 — Find which particle loses an H⁺.** That is the acid. HCl + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Cl⁻: HCl loses H⁺ → acid; H₂O gains it → base.

**Step 2 — Find the conjugate pairs.** When an acid loses H⁺ it becomes its **conjugate base** (HCl → Cl⁻). When a base gains H⁺ it becomes its **conjugate acid** (H₂O → H₃O⁺). The two members of a pair differ by **exactly one H⁺**.
**Step 3 — Ammonia now makes sense:** NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻. NH₃ accepts H⁺ → base; H₂O donates H⁺ → acid.
**Amphiprotic (amphoteric) species** can act as acid or base: H₂O, HCO₃⁻, HSO₄⁻, H₂PO₄⁻.
**Strength rule:** the stronger the acid, the weaker its conjugate base (HCl is strong, Cl⁻ has almost no tendency to take H⁺ back).

cards.title: Lewis theory, step by step (extension)
body: The textbook covers Arrhenius and Brønsted–Lowry. The **Lewis** theory is the broadest and is met again in Grade 12 and university entrance questions:
**Lewis acid = electron-pair acceptor. Lewis base = electron-pair donor.** The product has a new **coordinate (dative) bond**.
**Step 1 — Look for a lone pair.** The particle that gives the lone pair is the base (NH₃, H₂O, OH⁻, F⁻, Cl⁻).
**Step 2 — Look for an empty orbital.** The particle that receives the pair is the acid (H⁺, BF₃, AlCl₃, metal ions such as Ag⁺, Cu²⁺, Fe³⁺).
**Example:** BF₃ + :NH₃ → F₃B←NH₃. BF₃ has only 6 electrons around B, so it accepts the pair; there is no proton at all, so only the Lewis theory calls this an acid–base reaction.
Every Brønsted base is also a Lewis base (it needs a lone pair to take an H⁺), and H⁺ itself is a Lewis acid.

cards.title: 4.3.3 Indicators in a titration, step by step
body: An **acid–base indicator** is a dye (itself a weak acid or weak base) whose colour in its acid form differs from its colour in its base form. It changes colour as it **gains or loses H⁺ ions**, so it shows the **end point** of a titration.
**Step 1 — Fill the burette** with the solution of known concentration (e.g. NaOH). Read the starting volume at eye level, bottom of the meniscus.
**Step 2 — Pipette** an exact volume (e.g. 25.0 mL) of the other solution (e.g. HCl) into a conical flask.
**Step 3 — Add 2–3 drops of indicator.** Only a few drops: the indicator is itself a weak acid/base and too much would take part in the reaction.
**Step 4 — Run in the titrant** while swirling, quickly at first, then drop by drop near the end. A white tile under the flask helps you see the colour.
**Step 5 — Stop at the end point:** the first **permanent** colour change (e.g. colourless → pale pink with phenolphthalein).
**Step 6 — Read the final volume;** the difference is the titre. Repeat until two titres agree within 0.10 mL (concordant).

**End point vs equivalence point:** the **equivalence point** is when the acid and base have exactly reacted in the ratio of the equation; the **end point** is when the indicator changes colour. A good indicator makes the two almost the same.

steps.text: **Burette** holds the titrant (e.g. 0.100 M NaOH); read volumes at the bottom of the meniscus.

**End point:** the first permanent pale pink with phenolphthalein. Stop and read the burette.

cards.title: 4.4.4 Preparing salts, step by step
body: A salt contains the **positive ion of a base (or metal)** and the **negative ion of an acid**. Choose the method from **two questions**: Is the salt soluble in water? Which starting materials are safe and available?
**Method 1 — Neutralisation (acid + alkali).** For soluble salts of Na, K and NH₄. Titrate to find the exact volumes, mix again without indicator, evaporate and crystallise.
$$\mathrm{NaOH(aq)} + \mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaCl(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$$
**Method 2 — Acid + metal.** Only metals **more reactive than hydrogen** and not too reactive (Mg, Zn, Fe). Not Cu or Ag (no reaction); never Na or K (explosive).
$$\mathrm{Mg(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{MgSO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}(g)}$$
**Method 3 — Acid + carbonate or hydrogencarbonate.** Fizzing shows CO₂.
$$\mathrm{BaCO_{3}(s)} + 2\mathrm{HCl(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{BaCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} + \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}$$
$$\mathrm{HNO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{NaHCO_{3}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NaNO_{3}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)} + \mathrm{CO_{2}(g)}$$
**Method 4 — Acid + insoluble base (metal oxide), Activity 4.8.** Black CuO dissolves in warm dilute sulphuric acid to give a **blue** solution of copper(II) sulphate.
$$\mathrm{CuO(s)} + \mathrm{H_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{CuSO_{4}(aq)} + \mathrm{H_{2}O(l)}$$

**For methods 2–4 (excess solid):** add the solid to warm acid until no more dissolves (the acid is used up) → **filter** off the excess → **evaporate** to a saturated solution → **cool to crystallise** → filter and dry the crystals.
**Method 5 — Precipitation (double decomposition)** for **insoluble** salts: mix two solutions that contain the two ions, filter, wash with distilled water, dry.
$$\mathrm{BaCl_{2}(aq)} + \mathrm{Na_{2}SO_{4}(aq)} \rightarrow \mathrm{BaSO_{4}(s)} + 2\mathrm{NaCl(aq)}$$
**(Extra) Direct combination** of a metal and a non-metal: 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s); Fe(s) + S(s) → FeS(s).

body: Measuring the pH of a swimming pool is important: if the pH is outside the safe range (about 7.2–7.8) it can irritate the skin and allow bacteria to grow.
A universal indicator shows a series of colour changes at different pH values, so it indicates how acidic or alkaline the solution under investigation is.

cards.title: 4.5.1 Measuring pH, step by step
body: There are two common ways to measure pH: a **pH meter** and **indicators**. We measure pH in daily life too — for example swimming-pool water must stay at about pH 7.2–7.8, or it irritates skin and lets bacteria grow.

**A · The pH meter (accurate, a number):** a pair of electrodes (a glass probe) is connected to a meter that measures a small voltage. The voltage depends on [H⁺], and the meter is calibrated to show pH.
1. **Calibrate** with buffer solutions of known pH (e.g. pH 4 and 7).
2. **Rinse** the probe with distilled water and dip it into the sample.
3. **Wait** for a steady reading and record it (e.g. pH 6.84).
4. **Rinse** again before the next sample and store the probe wet.

**B · Indicators (quick, a colour, less precise):** an indicator has one colour in acid and another in base and changes within a small pH range. Many come from plants: red cabbage, roses, beetroot, grapes, sunflower petals. They are used as solutions or soaked onto paper.

cards.title: Step by step: The pH scale
body: **Step 1:** pH measures acidity: pH = −log[H⁺]. The scale runs from 0 to 14 at 25 °C.
**Step 2:** pH < 7 acidic, pH = 7 neutral (pure water), pH > 7 basic (alkaline).
**Step 3:** Each unit of pH is a factor of 10 in [H⁺]: pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4.
**Step 4:** pH + pOH = 14, where pOH = −log[OH⁻].
**Step 5:** Measure pH with universal indicator (colour chart), pH paper or a pH meter (most accurate).
**Example:** [H⁺] = 1 × 10⁻³ M → pH = 3 (acidic). A 0.01 M NaOH solution: [OH⁻] = 10⁻² → pOH = 2 → pH = 14 − 2 = 12 (basic).

units.intro: Energy is conserved. In chemistry we track heat. Breaking bonds *takes* energy (endothermic). Making bonds *releases* energy (exothermic). The sign of the whole reaction is which side wins.

5.1.1 Law of Conservation of Energy
body: All matter possesses energy in one form or another.
The different forms of kinetic energy include thermal energy and electrical energy.
The different forms of potential energy include chemical energy and gravitational energy.
The most common form of energy change in chemical reactions is heat change, and thus the major part of this sub-unit will be concerned with the heat changes that accompany chemical reactions.

cards.title: 5.1.3 Bond Breaking and Bond Formation
body: Chemical reactions usually involve the making or breaking of chemical bonds.
The energy of the product molecules may therefore be greater or less than the energy of the reactant molecules.

cards.title: 5.1.4 Enthalpy and ΔH, step by step
body: Every substance stores energy in its bonds. The **heat content** of a substance at constant pressure is called its **enthalpy, H**. We cannot measure H itself, but we can measure the **change**, ΔH (“delta H”), during a reaction.
$$\Delta H = H_{\text{products}} - H_{\text{reactants}} = H_P - H_R$$
**Step 1 — Bonds in the reactants are broken.** This never happens by itself: energy must be **supplied** (absorbed), so this stage is endothermic.
**Step 2 — New bonds in the products are formed.** This happens by itself and energy is **released**, so this stage is exothermic.
**Step 3 — Compare the two amounts:**
$$\Delta H = \sum(\text{energy to break bonds}) - \sum(\text{energy released forming bonds})$$
If more energy is released than absorbed, ΔH is **negative** (exothermic, H_P < H_R). If more is absorbed, ΔH is **positive** (endothermic, H_P > H_R).
**Unit:** kilojoules per mole, **kJ/mol** — per mole of reaction as written in the equation.
**Activity 5.5 explained:** adding quicklime (CaO) to water makes the beaker hot. Heat flows **from the beaker to your hand**: the reaction CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ releases energy, so ΔH is negative.

cards.title: Model: break bonds, then make bonds (H₂ + Cl₂ → 2HCl)

steps.text: **Break:** H–H (436 kJ) and Cl–Cl (243 kJ) need 679 kJ in total — the energy goes **up** to separate atoms.
**Make:** two H–Cl bonds form (2 × 432 = 864 kJ) — energy comes **out**.
**Net:** ΔH = 679 − 864 = **−185 kJ** per mole of reaction: the products are lower, the reaction is exothermic.

cards.title: Exothermic or endothermic? Step by step
body: The **system** is the reacting chemicals; the **surroundings** are everything else (the beaker, the water, the air, your hand).
**Step 1 — Bonds.** Breaking bonds **absorbs** energy; making bonds **releases** energy.
**Step 2 — Compare.** If more energy is released making the new bonds than was absorbed breaking the old ones, the reaction is **exothermic**; otherwise it is **endothermic**.

**Step 3 — Sign of ΔH.** Exothermic: heat leaves the system, **ΔH < 0** (negative), the surroundings get **warmer**. Endothermic: heat enters the system, **ΔH > 0** (positive), the surroundings get **colder**.
$$\Delta H = H_{\text{products}} - H_{\text{reactants}}$$
**Step 4 — Check with a thermometer:** temperature of the mixture rises → exothermic; falls → endothermic.

cards.title: Everyday examples
head: Exothermic (ΔH negative, gets hot)
Endothermic (ΔH positive, gets cold or needs heating)
rows: Burning methane (natural gas), wood, charcoal: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O, ΔH = −890 kJ
Respiration in our cells (the reverse of photosynthesis)
Thermal decomposition: CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂, ΔH = +178 kJ (lime kilns)
Neutralisation: H⁺ + OH⁻ → H₂O, ΔH = −57.1 kJ
Dissolving NH₄NO₃ or NH₄Cl in water (instant cold packs)
Slaking quicklime: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (very hot)
Dissolving NaOH or concentrated H₂SO₄ in water
Melting ice, boiling water, sweat evaporating (cools the skin)
Rusting of iron, condensation of steam, freezing of water
Baking soda + vinegar (the mixture feels cold); cooking an egg

steps.text: **Exothermic:** the products are **lower** than the reactants. The drop is ΔH (negative): energy given out.
**Endothermic:** the products are **higher** than the reactants. The rise is ΔH (positive): energy taken in.
**Activation energy, Ea:** from the reactants up to the top of the hump. Even exothermic reactions must climb it first (a match is needed to light gas).
A **catalyst** gives a lower hump (smaller Ea) but does **not** change ΔH.

cards.title: How to draw an energy-level diagram, step by step
body: 1. Draw a vertical axis labelled **energy (enthalpy, H)** and a horizontal axis **reaction progress**.
2. Draw a short line for the **reactants** on the left.
3. Draw the **products** on the right: **lower** for exothermic, **higher** for endothermic. Write the formulas on the lines.
4. Join them with a curve that rises to a **hump** (the activated complex).
5. Add arrows: **Ea** from reactants up to the top of the hump; **ΔH** from reactants to products (pointing down for exothermic, up for endothermic). Write its value with the sign.
**Reverse reaction:** ΔH changes sign, and \(E_a(\text{reverse}) = E_a(\text{forward}) - \Delta H\).

cards.title: Worked example: burning methane
cards.problem: CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ/mol. (a) Is it exo- or endothermic? (b) Describe its energy diagram. (c) How much heat is released by burning 8.0 g of methane (M = 16 g/mol)?

steps.text: (a) ΔH is negative → **exothermic**.
(b) Products (CO₂ + 2H₂O) are drawn 890 kJ **below** the reactants (CH₄ + 2O₂), with a hump between them; ΔH arrow points down.
(c) Moles of CH₄ = \(\dfrac{8.0}{16} = 0.50\text{ mol}\)
Heat released = \(0.50 \times 890 = 445\text{ kJ}\)

cards.problem: N₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2NO(g), ΔH = +180 kJ. (a) Exo or endo? (b) What is ΔH for 2NO → N₂ + O₂? (c) Why does NO form in a car engine or during lightning but not in ordinary air?

steps.text: (a) ΔH positive → **endothermic**; the products are 180 kJ above the reactants.
(b) The reverse reaction has the opposite sign: ΔH = −180 kJ.
(c) The reaction needs a large energy input (and a high Ea); the very high temperatures in engines and lightning supply it.

cards.answer: Endothermic; reverse ΔH = −180 kJ; needs very high temperature.

cards.problem: On an energy diagram the reactants are at 50 kJ, the top of the hump at 150 kJ and the products at 20 kJ. Find Ea, ΔH and Ea of the reverse reaction.

steps.text: Ea (forward) = 150 − 50 = 100 kJ
ΔH = H(products) − H(reactants) = 20 − 50 = −30 kJ (exothermic)
Ea (reverse) = 150 − 20 = 130 kJ

cards.answer: Ea = 100 kJ, ΔH = −30 kJ, Ea(reverse) = 130 kJ

cards.title: Types of Heat of Reaction and Heat Changes
body: Main types: heat of combustion, solution, neutralisation, formation, fusion, vaporisation. Thermochemical equation prints ΔH next to the balanced reaction. Units: kJ / kJ mol⁻¹.

cards.title: Types of heat of reaction, step by step
body: Each “heat of …” is ΔH for a stated process and a stated amount — usually **1 mol** of the substance named. Read the definition carefully: it tells you what goes on the left and right of the equation.
**Heat of combustion:** heat released when **1 mol** of a substance burns **completely** in oxygen. Always **negative**. CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(l), ΔH = −890 kJ/mol.
**Heat of solution:** enthalpy change when **1 mol** of a substance dissolves in a large amount of water. Can be **negative** (NaOH, about −44 kJ/mol) or **positive** (NH₄NO₃, about +26 kJ/mol).

**Heat of neutralisation:** heat released when an acid and a base react to form **1 mol of water**. For any strong acid + strong base: H⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq) → H₂O(l), ΔH = **−57.1 kJ/mol**. A weak acid gives a smaller value because some energy is used to ionise it.

**Heat of formation:** enthalpy change when **1 mol of a compound** forms from its **elements** in their standard states. C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −393 kJ/mol; C(s) + 2S(s) → CS₂(l), ΔH = +117 kJ/mol. The heat of formation of an element is zero.
**Heat of fusion:** heat **absorbed** when 1 mol of solid melts at its melting point. H₂O(s) → H₂O(l), ΔH = +6.01 kJ/mol.
**Heat of vaporisation:** heat **absorbed** when 1 mol of liquid turns into vapour at its boiling point. H₂O(l) → H₂O(g), ΔH = +40.7 kJ/mol.

Water formed = 0.050 mol

(b) Acid + base → 1 mol water → **heat of neutralisation**.
(c) Liquid → vapour, 1 mol → **heat of vaporisation**.

body: Sketch two horizontal lines (reactants, products) and a hump (Ea). If products sit lower, shade ΔH downward and write “exo, ΔH < 0”. If products sit higher, ΔH upward, endo. A catalyst cuts the hump, not the gap between the two lines.
